source.title: UMA: A Family of Universal Models for Atoms
source.authors: Brandon M. Wood; Misko Dzamba; Xiang Fu; Meng Gao; Muhammed Shuaibi; Luis Barroso-Luque; Kareem Abdelmaqsoud; Vahe Gharakhanyan; John R. Kitchin; Daniel S. Levine; Kyle Michel; Anuroop Sriram; Taco Cohen; Abhishek Das; Ammar Rizvi; Sushree Jagriti Sahoo; Zachary W. Ulissi; C. Zitnick

record.file_problem: The text contains the full paper and appendices; no truncation or garbling that prevents reading the scaling results.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures empirical scaling relations for atomistic models, extending scaling-law tests to a different modality and loss setting.
record.gate_note: Relevant results are the pretraining scaling experiments: validation loss, Iso-FLOPs compute-optimal fits, and their reported limits. Benchmark scores, MoLE expert-count comparisons, and other model evaluations are not rows because they do not measure the scaling-law claims at issue.
record.test_reason: Iso-FLOPs sweeps (10^18–10^20 FLOPs) of equivariant atomistic models (dense and 8-expert MoLE) fit power laws for compute-optimal parameters, data (atoms) and loss versus N*. This tests whether the scaling-law form carries over to a non-text modality (V5). It does not test the language-model-specific versions (V1–V4, V6, V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors report that dense and MoLE atomistic models show log-linear scaling over 10^18–10^20 FLOPs, and they used the fits to pick a ~700M-parameter compute-optimal dense model (UMA-L) for an extrapolated O(10^22) FLOPs budget. They report that MoLE matches dense loss with ~2.5× fewer active parameters, but this advantage shrinks at larger sizes (possibly a data limit). They also report that training for too many epochs causes overfitting and departures from log-linear scaling.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Iso-FLOPs experiments and power-law fitting in a related scaling-law framework, but studies equivariant atomistic models and total validation loss rather than language models and held-out cross-entropy; the data axis is atoms rather than tokens.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted coefficients differ between dense and MoLE architectures. Training for too many epochs can cause overfitting and significant departures from log-linear scaling. The scaling-law experiments are restricted to pretraining.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss improves strongly from 1 to 8 MoLE experts, less at 32, and negligibly at 128 (UMA-S, Figure 2 right bottom).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In atomistic MoLE models, loss gains from adding experts saturate.

fits_no_version.finding: MoLE's advantage over dense (Δ≈2.5× fewer active parameters at equal loss) shrinks at larger sizes, with near convergence at 700M active parameters; authors hypothesise a dataset-size limit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benefits of sparse/expert capacity in atomistic models diminish as models grow toward the data limit.

record.problems: Scaling experiments cover 10^18–10^20 FLOPs, while the estimated pretraining compute budget is O(10^22) FLOPs; the larger-budget estimates are therefore extrapolations. Scaling laws were tested only in pretraining, not energy-conserving fine-tuning. The authors report overfitting-related departures, and the printed MoLE dataset exponent point estimate is outside its stated bootstrap bounds.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling-law outcomes were reported in the remaining text. General benchmark scores and MoLE expert-count comparisons were left out because they do not directly measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: No language-model loss; the atomistic analogue is recorded under V5.
No test of extrapolation. The O(10^22) FLOPs budget and ~700M size are extrapolated from 10^18–10^20 fits, but the extrapolated loss is never checked against an actual run.
No language-model parameter/token allocation; the atomistic allocation fits are recorded under V5.
Depth and width are not varied at fixed parameter count.
Benchmark performance is not related to scale or loss in a fitted way.
No comparison of fitting or setup choices for language-model laws.

Only atomistic pretraining is covered; no image/video models. Scaling was explicitly not studied for energy-conserving fine-tuning. No transfer scaling. Repeated data is covered only qualitatively (r8). The fitted range spans only about two orders of magnitude of compute.

missing.what: The authors report that fitting the 5-parameter L(N,D) by LBFGS and fitting loss vs N* gave similar results, but the LBFGS fit was more sensitive to hyperparameters. This is a fitting-method sensitivity statement.
missing.versions: V5 (fit-dependence in the atomistic setting; would be V7 if not LM-restricted)

missing.what: The iso-FLOP validation-loss curves themselves (loss values at each compute budget, and the parabola-fit minima) are not recorded as rows.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked rows to V3 and V7, but those versions concern language-model parameter/token allocation and published LM laws. This study is atomistic (data in atoms), so its scaling results go to V5 only. Rows r7 and r9 compare the authors' own MoLE method with dense and are not scaling-law measures. The fitted compute range is two orders of magnitude, and α+β=1 is imposed by C≈κND.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests atomistic models, not language models, and does not measure held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy.

It fits scaling relations over smaller compute runs and uses them to estimate optimal sizes, but does not report a direct test of whether those fits predict the loss of runs orders of magnitude larger.
The allocation is between model parameters and dataset size in atoms, not language-model tokens; the study does not test language-model allocations.
It compares dense and MoLE architectures, but does not systematically vary depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The tested setting is atomistic-model pretraining; it does not test image or video models, repeated data, or fine-tuning and transfer scaling laws.
The study does not measure whether downstream task performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.
It reports architecture-specific fit coefficients and overfitting-related departures, but does not systematically vary parameter-counting conventions, data, schedules, or fitting methods.

rows.subject: dense
rows.size_stated: Dense model class; individual scaling-sweep sizes not stated
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law to Iso-FLOPs minima for compute-optimal model size.
rows.measure: Exponent α for log(N*(C)) = α log(C) + A
rows.note: Fits use the dense architecture. The reported point estimate indicates model size grows faster than dataset size in this fit.
rows.check: V3 names language-model parameter/token allocation; this is an atomistic model with data in atoms, so it bears on V5, not V3 or V7. Note α+β=1 is forced by C≈κND.

rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law to Iso-FLOPs minima for optimal dataset size.
rows.measure: Exponent β for log(D*(C)) = β log(C) + B
rows.note: The dataset-size fit is in atoms, not tokens.
rows.check: Same as r1: atomistic setting, so V5 only.

rows.subject: MoLE (8 expert)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law to Iso-FLOPs minima for compute-optimal model size.
rows.measure: Exponent α for log(N*(C)) = α log(C) + A
rows.note: The scaling-law experiments used the UMA-M settings for the MoLE model.
rows.check: Atomistic MoLE fit, so V5 only. The dense-vs-MoLE α intervals overlap (0.57–0.65 vs 0.49–0.59), so this is weak evidence of architecture dependence.

rows.subject: MoLE (8 expert)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law to Iso-FLOPs minima for optimal dataset size.
rows.measure: Exponent β for log(D*(C)) = β log(C) + B
rows.note: The point estimate is recorded as printed, although it lies outside the printed bootstrap interval.
rows.check: V5 only. The printed point estimate 0.44 lies outside its printed bound (0.39, 0.43). Since α+β=1 (0.56+0.44), the interval is likely a typo.

relationships.condition: Atomistic (equivariant GNN) pretraining, dense and 8-expert MoLE, 10^18–10^20 FLOPs, ~1 epoch
relationships.reason: Compute-optimal N* and D* follow power laws in compute (α 0.61/0.56, β 0.39/0.44), and minimum loss follows a power law in N* (α̂ −0.29/−0.25) (r1–r6).
relationships.display_finding: Dense and MoLE optimal parameter exponents are 0.61 and 0.56, data exponents are 0.39 and 0.44, and loss-versus-optimal-size exponents are −0.29 and −0.25.

relationships.reason: Authors state that overfitting from too many epochs significantly departs from log-linear scaling, so they capped training at 2–3 epochs (r8). This is qualitative only.
relationships.display_finding: Too many epochs caused overfitting and substantial departures from log-linear scaling, leading the authors to cap training at 2–3 epochs.
